paras: The lynching of James Hagley was the shooting death of a Black man at Alma, Arkansas, on the night of July 2-3, 1888, after he was taken from the town jail at midnight. He had been held on an accusation of attempting to assault a 12-year-old girl, and according to a wire dispatch he was tied to a tree and "slowly shot to pieces." The killing reached distant newspapers only as a one-sentence telegraphic item.

The victim, described as "colored," was named James Hagley in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and James Bagley in the Press and Daily Dakotaian of Yankton. He was in jail at Alma charged, in the dispatch's words, with "attempting to assault" or "attempting to outrage" a girl aged 12, whose name was printed as Belie Simms in one paper and Belle Simmons in the other.

According to the dispatch dated Alma, July 3, he was taken from the jail at midnight. His captors tied him to a tree and shot him to death. The reports do not say who took him, how many people were involved, or whether officers were present.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

Both known reports reproduce a single wire dispatch almost word for word, differing only in the spelling of the two names. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union ran it on July 4 as one line among its "Telegraphic Brevities," between items on King Milan's separation suit and a Yale rower. The Yankton paper printed it the next day under the heading "Shot to Death." Neither paper commented on the killing, and both gave the accusation as its cause.
The victim's surname appears as Hagley in the Sacramento paper and Bagley in the Yankton paper, and since both copies descend from one dispatch neither spelling has better standing.

reader.title: Lynching of James Hagley
bases: A man held in jail on an accusation was taken out at midnight and shot to death while tied to a tree (A1, A2).

The victim was taken from jail and shot to death over an accusation of attempted assault, an extralegal killing under a pretext of punishment (A1, A2); neither report names the killers or says how many there were, so the group of three or more is not stated.
Both reports carry the same wording of one Alma dispatch of July 3, with only spelling differences in the names, so they are not independent accounts (A1, A2).
